title: Find Mode in Binary Search Tree
description: Brute force to optimized: hash map counting versus in-order traversal with a running streak, exploiting sorted adjacency of duplicates.

content.title: Find Mode in Binary Search Tree

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given the root of a BST that may contain duplicate values, return all the mode(s) (the value(s) that appear with the highest frequency) in the tree, in any order.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.text: Since in-order traversal of a BST visits values in sorted order, all occurrences of the SAME value are always adjacent in this traversal. This means a running "current streak length" (reset whenever the value changes) captures every value's frequency without needing a hash map.

blocks.title: Analogy: Counting the Longest Run of Identical Cards in a Sorted Deck
blocks.text: Picture a deck of cards already sorted by rank, possibly with duplicates, and wanting to know which rank(s) appear most often. Since duplicates are always adjacent in sorted order, simply tracking how long the CURRENT run of identical cards is, and comparing it to the longest run seen so far, finds the answer without any separate counting per rank.

blocks.caption: In-order traversal is sorted, so equal values form adjacent runs, tracked with a simple running streak

blocks.text: Result: [2]. In-order gives 1,2,2; value 2 appears twice, the highest frequency.

Before counting every value's frequency in a hash map, notice that in-order traversal already groups equal values adjacently, so a simple running streak counter (reset when the value changes) tracks frequency without any auxiliary structure.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: In-order traversal visits BST values in sorted order, so all occurrences of a given value appear consecutively.

Observation 2: Tracking a running "current streak" (incremented when the current value equals the previous, reset to 1 otherwise) directly gives that value's frequency as it is being traversed.

Observation 3: Comparing the current streak to a running "max streak so far" identifies the mode(s): if the current streak EXCEEDS the max, it becomes the new sole mode; if it EQUALS the max, it is added to the mode list.

Observation 4: A single in-order pass, with no hash map, correctly identifies all modes using only O(1) extra space (beyond the output and recursion stack).
This leads to an in-order traversal tracking a running streak count and a running max streak, updating the mode list whenever the current streak matches or exceeds the max.
Traverse the tree, counting occurrences of every value in a hash map, then find the maximum count and collect all values matching it.
Why the code is written this way

items: A hash map directly counts occurrences of every value, correct regardless of tree structure.
This uses O(n) extra space, more than necessary given the BST's sorted in-order traversal property.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n).
Space: O(n) for the hash map.
Limitation: since equal values are always adjacent in in-order traversal, a running streak counter achieves O(1) extra space instead of O(n) for a hash map.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Since in-order traversal groups equal values adjacently, a running "current streak" (reset when the value changes from the previous one) tracks each value's frequency directly. Comparing this to a running "max streak" identifies whether the current value becomes the new sole mode or joins the existing set of modes, all without a hash map.
In-order traversal, tracking prev value, current streak, and max streak; update the mode list based on comparing the current streak to the max streak at each node.

Since in-order traversal groups all occurrences of a value adjacently, the running streak counter correctly measures each value's total frequency as it is traversed, without needing a hash map. Comparing this streak to the running maximum correctly identifies the current mode set: a new higher streak resets the mode list to just this value, while a tied streak adds this value alongside the existing modes.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n).
Space: O(height) recursion depth, O(1) extra beyond the output.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "find the most frequent value(s) in a BST", think: in-order traversal groups duplicates adjacently, track a running streak instead of a hash map.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Hash map counting costs O(n) time and space; the running streak approach costs O(n) time and only O(height) extra space, the more efficient solution for this BST-specific problem.

items: Pattern: exploit BST in-order traversal being sorted to replace a hash map with a running streak counter.
Core Idea: track a running streak (reset on value change) and a max streak; update the mode list when the streak matches or exceeds the max.
Space: O(n) for the hash map versus O(height) extra for the running streak.
Most Important Observation: BST in-order traversal groups all duplicate values adjacently, eliminating the need for a hash map.
Interview Difficulty: a well-known problem with a notable O(1)-space follow-up.
One line memory trick: in-order traversal, track a running streak and max streak, no hash map needed.
